newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Xerox unveils digital copiers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Xerox unveils digital copiers.

text.p: Xerox Corp. Tuesday launched a family of four high-speed digital copiers that can be linked to computer networks, as the first step in its overall strategy to embrace the digital world.

Xerox rolled out four black-and-white digital copiers, with color models to come in a few weeks, as it seeks to transform the copier -- a stand-alone piece of office equipment into an integral part of a networked computing environment.
Analysts said digital products will drive Xerox's future growth and they will be the majority of revenues by 2000-2001.
Xerox Chief Executive Paul Allaire told a press conference that the company had reached "a digital critical mass" and has "embraced a digital future" with these new machines.

Xerox unveiled four Document Centre black and white copiers, which can be upgraded from stand-alone copiers to multi-function office systems that can print, fax and scan electronic documents created on a PC or a computer network.

"These products are a cornerstone (of their strategy) of where Xerox wants to be in the year 2000," said John Dunkle, president of Workgroup Strategic Services Inc. "I think Xerox is going to be a very, very different company than what we think of Xerox today, in the year 2000."
Allaire said he expected revenues for the new products to reach $2 billion "over time."

Allaire also said he expected the new digital products to be more successful than Xerox's DocuTech high speed copier family, which it introduced in 1990. That family of copiers had about $1.8 billion in revenues last year.

"We expect it to be more important than DocuTech," Allaire said, adding that it took about six years for the DocuTech to reach its current revenue stream. "That gives you an idea," he said, when asked about how long it will take the new digital copiers to reach $2 billion in revenues.
Xerox also plans to roll out color digital copiers in a few weeks, as part of its vision of a "digital future."
"Digital is growing in excess of 20 percent every year," Allaire said, adding that sales of digital products will become an increasingly bigger part of its overall revenues.
This compares with Xerox's total revenue growth of 7 percent in the fourth quarter. Xerox is expected to report first quarter results on April 22.
Currently, digital revenues make up over 30 percent of Xerox's revenues, while over 50 percent are from its stand-alone, analog copier business.

Xerox has invested over $500 million over a period of years in the development of this next generation of products, but Allaire emphasized that it will not abandon its analog copiers, which cannot be hooked up to digital devices.

"There are some instances where a light lens copier still makes sense," Allaire said, adding that Xerox already has introduced five analog copiers earlier this year and more launches are expected this year.

Of the new digital copiers, two models are available immediately, the Xerox Document Centre 220 and 230 models, which can copy 20 and 30 pages per minute, respectively, are currently available with a facsimile upgrade in the United States, Canada and parts of Europe. Networked versions will be offered in the fourth quarter 1997.

The 220 model's list price is $8,600 and the 230 is listed at $10,500. The other two models, the Document Centre 240 and 265 will be available in the second half of 1997. Xerox stock rose $1.375 to $56.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
